details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: How should labor, energy, materials, and machine_time be weighted in the resource denominator — for example, should a 10% cut in energy count the same as a 10% cut in labor hours, or do you want a cost-weighted aggregate (e.g., total €/shift)?
flags.resolution: Apply equal fractional weights across all four resource types, each normalised by its respective baseline consumption value for the shift, so no single resource dominates the denominator.

flags.question: The formal priority field lists HumanWellbeing above efficiency, but the raw intent ordering puts delivered_value_per_resource first — if raising the fatigue index to 0.39 (just under the hard limit) yields a 15% efficiency gain, should the optimiser accept it?
flags.resolution: Treat HumanWellbeing as the binding top priority: fatigue and noise hard constraints are inviolable, and efficiency is maximised only within the remaining feasible space.

flags.field: delivered_value_per_resource (no saturation ceiling / upper bound on resource push)
flags.question: Is there a maximum machine utilisation rate or labour allocation ceiling beyond which you would not want the optimiser to push — for instance, capping machine utilisation at 85% of rated capacity — even if exceeding it would improve the efficiency KPI?
flags.resolution: Cap machine utilisation at 90% of rated capacity and disallow overtime; the optimiser must improve efficiency within standard shift resources and may not saturate any single resource type above 90% of its rated limit.

flags.question: Should the 80 dB(A) limit apply as a single time-averaged Leq over the full shift, or as a rolling Leq over shorter intervals (e.g., 15-minute windows per ISO 9612), so a noisy burst cannot be masked by quieter periods?
flags.resolution: Enforce the 80 dB(A) limit as a 15-minute rolling Leq throughout the shift to prevent prolonged high-noise exposures that a shift-long average would otherwise obscure.

flags.field: operator_fatigue_index (measurement timing — end-of-shift snapshot vs. continuous)
flags.question: Must the fatigue index remain at or below 0.4 continuously throughout the shift, or is it only checked at end-of-shift — because a single end-of-shift sample could miss a mid-shift peak that recovers before the shift ends?
flags.resolution: Enforce the fatigue constraint continuously (worst-case value across all sampling intervals during the shift), not only at end-of-shift, to prevent unsafe mid-shift fatigue peaks.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Schedule S1 was authored under an assumed demand of 52.0 UPH. With actual demand at 62.4 UPH (+20%), the volume of work queued per time window has increased proportionally. Current system throughput stands at only 40.7 UPH — already 21.7% below the original planned rate and 34.8% below real demand. The cumulative unit shortfall compounds each cycle: every hour the system runs at 40.7 UPH against a 62.4 UPH requirement generates a backlog of ~21.7 units. This widening production deficit directly erodes the DeadlineGap metric (time remaining minus time required to clear queue), pushing its margin into breach territory. The contract's completion horizon was sized for 52 UPH throughput; the demand surge invalidates that sizing without a corresponding schedule revision or throughput uplift.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately escalate to the schedule owner and production supervisor. Options in priority order: (1) trigger a schedule re-plan (S1 revision) that recalculates cycle allocation for 62.4 UPH demand; (2) authorize a controlled robot speed increase to close the throughput gap — monitor noise_db (currently 77.8) and energy_kwh (currently 401.0) against their respective ceilings as speed rises; (3) if throughput cannot be recovered within the current phase window, negotiate a deadline extension or partial-delivery milestone with the downstream customer to avoid a hard deadline miss.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: FatigueIndex is the most severely violated constraint (0.6001 vs limit 0.4, margin -0.200). human_cycle_rate_multiplier is the direct and sole primary driver of operator fatigue accumulation. At 1.15 the human is working at 115% of nominal pace; reducing to 0.80 lowers the biomechanical load rate by ~30%, which should bring FatigueIndex from 0.6001 into the feasible region (estimated ~0.42 or below depending on baseline). Robot speed changes have negligible effect on fatigue, making this the only targeted lever for that constraint.

r2 is running at maximum speed (1.0), making it the dominant noise emitter in the cell. Noise violations are measured in dB which combine logarithmically from all sources, but the highest-speed robot contributes disproportionately to the noise floor. Reducing r2 by 18% (1.0 → 0.82) reduces its mechanical and aerodynamic noise output; this adjustment alone is estimated to lower the aggregate cell noise by 3-4 dB, the largest single-parameter gain available for the Noise constraint.

After reducing r2 to 0.82, the remaining noise margin gap (~1-2 dB) requires an additional reduction from r1. Bringing r1 from 0.9 to 0.82 (change of -0.08, smaller than the r2 adjustment) harmonises both robots at 0.82 speed fraction, removing r1 as a secondary noise contributor and providing the incremental dB reduction needed to clear the 80.0 dB ceiling. The symmetric speed reduction also minimises cycle-time imbalance between robot stations, reducing pipeline stall risk.

details.conflict: A 20.0% demand surge has produced a schedule that violates two human-centric constraints simultaneously. FatigueIndex reached 0.6001 against a hard ceiling of 0.40 (excess: +0.2001, ~50% over limit), and ambient Noise reached 84.9 dB against a ceiling of 80.0 dB (excess: +4.9 dB). Because both violations are classified as human-centric under the CBPA governance policy, the schedule was automatically rejected and escalated. No feasible schedule exists at current demand levels without either reducing throughput or obtaining a temporary, time-bounded relaxation of one or both limits. Immediate manager action is required to unblock production.
options: Option 1 — Partial Demand Fulfilment with Split Shifts (Preserve All Human Constraints)
Option 2 — Engineering Noise Controls with Temporary Noise Limit Waiver (Relax Noise Only)
Option 3 — Dual Temporary Waiver with Compensatory Controls (Relax Both Constraints, Highest Risk)

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0.00% with dual critical violations (FatigueIndex at 100% and Noise at 80% violation probability) under a +20% demand surge indicates the current parameter space is fundamentally infeasible. MICRO adjustments of +/-5% speed or +/-10% cycle rate cannot address a zero-feasibility scenario with both ergonomic and acoustic constraints severely violated simultaneously. MESO policy switching alone is insufficient because the demand surge (+20%) combined with already-moderate robot speeds (r1=0.70, r2=0.65) means any policy family that accommodates the demand increase will worsen fatigue and noise, while any policy that protects those constraints cannot meet demand. The constraint violations are not isolated or marginal — FatigueIndex is at full violation, suggesting workers are being pushed to physiological limits regardless of minor parameter changes. Full replanning from L1-L2 is required to fundamentally restructure the schedule, potentially redistributing workload across shifts, introducing rest intervals, reassigning tasks between robots and humans, or adjusting throughput targets.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Zero feasibility probability with 100% FatigueIndex violation means the current schedule architecture is intrinsically infeasible under the demand surge — no parameter tweak or policy switch can reconcile maximum ergonomic stress with a 20% production increase without a ground-up replan.
